During the period from October 2,	1955, to
January 25, 1956, how many persons, by provinces or by regions, were refused unemployment insurance benefits by reason of their inability to meet the requirements of section 45 (2) of the Unemployment Insurance Act?
[ Mr. Campney.]
The answer to that part of the question is this. In the period October 2, 1955, to January 31, 1956, 99,462 claimants failed to qualify for regular benefit by reason of section 45 (2). The breakdown can only be given by regions:
Atlantic region	 14,456
Quebec region	 29,664
Ontario region	 27,622
Prairie region	 16,244
Pacific region	 11,476
99,462
Of these claimants 90,269 had sufficient contributions to qualify for seasonal benefit of ten weeks or more.
The second part of the question is:
By provinces or by regions, how many of these cases have been reviewed?
The answer is as follows. For the purposes of the re-examination of contribution records, all the 99,462 claimants who had failed to qualify for regular benefit were notified to present their insurance books to the local office.
Twenty-two thousand two hundred and ninety (22,290) of these failed to respond and it is assumed they are not interested at this time. It is believed the majority are gainfully employed.
The remainder, 77,172, were re-examined and these were located as shown in the following table. I might interject here that 64,484 of these had already established claims for seasonal benefit prior to the commencement of the re-examination. The breakdown of the 77,172 is as follows:
Atlantic region	 12,489
Quebec region	 22,881
Ontario region	 15,268
Prairie region	 16,354
Pacific region	 10,180
77,172
The third part of the question is:
By provinces or by regions, how many of these persons have been put on unemployment insurance benefits as a result of the reinterpretation of section 119 (b) of the Unemployment Insurance Act, announced by the Minister of Labour on January 25, 1956?
The answer is as follows. The number put on regular or seasonal benefit following re-examination, which applied the new interpretation of 119(b), was 6,002 and these were located as follows:

Ontario region	 983

6,002
The re-examination of this group also resulted in another 6,000 seasonal benefit

claimants establishing an additional entitlement to regular benefit for varying periods prior to the commencement of their seasonal benefit periods.
On March 28, the hon. member asked if I would be in a position at this time to state whether or not I consider it desirable to amend section 45 (2) of the act. I would like to point out that section 45 (2) contains one of the basic conditions underlying entitlement to benefit. To fully appraise its total effect, a lengthy period of operation in necessary in order to provide sufficient data by which conclusions may be reached. The act has been in force for six months, and this is not considered to be a period of sufficient duration for appraisal purposes.
I think, however, that a significant trend is indicated by the most recent statistics. These figures show that, while active claimants at the end of February, 1956, were about 18 per cent lower than at the end of the same month in 1955, benefit payments in February, 1956, were only 10 per cent less than in the previous year. Indications are that this trend continued through March.
I wish to assure my hon. friend that I have a keen interest in the application of section 45 (2) as well as in many other sections of the new act, and, as soon as a proper appraisal can be made, the house will be informed of the results.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S.S.R.-APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 29, 1956

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-U.S.S.R.-APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 29, 1956
speechtext:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament approve the ratification by Canada of the agreement on trade between Canada and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, signed at Ottawa on February 29, 1956, and that this house do approve the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on February 29 I took pleasure in announcing the conclusion of a trade agreement between Canada and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. I stated at that time that an opportunity would be provided for a debate on this trade agreement in advance of its ratification. Now that the time has come for this debate, it is appropriate for me to make a few remarks.
One of the principal features of this agreement is the exchange of most-favourednation treatment between the two governments. The effect of this is to put Canadian commercial relations with the U.S.S.R. on a basis comparable to our relations with most other countries. Hon. members no doubt understand what is meant by "mostfavoured-nation treatment". In the time-honoured terminology of the tariff, this means that imports from a particular country will be treated no less favourably than those from any other country. Most-favourednation treatment has reference to tariffs and related matters in the field of commercial
policy. Most-favoured-nation treatment does not entitle another country to any unique advantages but merely guarantees that the country will not be discriminated against in trade matters.
Imports into Canada from the U.S.S.R. are now admitted, under the provisional application of this agreement, at the rates of the most-favoured-nation tariff schedule. Mostfavoured-nation treatment does not involve, of course, the application of the British preferential rates of duty to imports from the U.S.S.R.
In our country, most trade is conducted under private auspices. Most decisions regarding purchases and sales abroad are made by private people. The government, of course, plays a most important part. In promoting trade relations with other countries, by tariff policy and by other means the government establishes a framework of arrangements to expedite trade and sometimes to regulate trade. It is an inherent feature, however, of our business system and of the government's policy that the Canadian people shall be as free as possible to decide what they will buy.
It follows that in negotiating a mostfavoured-nation agreement with the U.S.S.R., or any other country, the government does not attempt to stipulate that certain things shall be imported into Canada and that other things shall not be imported. Aside from the effects of the tariff, such matters are not in general subject to governmental regulation. Canada does not undertake in this agreement, therefore, to purchase any specific goods from the U.S.S.R. The major undertaking given by Canada is that imports from the U.S.S.R. may compete on equal terms with imports from other countries in the most-favoured-nation category.
Under the agreement, Canada also receives most-favoured-nation treatment from the U.S.S.R. The meaning of this undertaking is quite different in a state trading country than it is in a private enterprise country such as ours. Soviet purchases and sales abroad are made within a framework of governmental policy by officials of state trading organizations. Accordingly, the agreement includes a general undertaking whereby each government accords most-favoured-nation treatment with respect to sales or purchases involving exports or imports. This clause offers to Canadian exporters a prospect of competing on commercial terms for sales to Soviet state trading organizations.
Certain escape clauses are included in the agreement, to be used if unanticipated difficulties should arise. These escape clauses are comparable in their effect with those contained in the general agreement on tariffs

and trade. For example, provision is made for the imposition of import restrictions, even on a discriminatory basis if necessary, in the event of balance of payments difficulties. In this connection, I should also mention the letter from the Canadian government which forms a part of the agreement, reserving the right to establish values for import duty if any Russian products should enter Canada in such increased quantities as to cause serious injury to domestic producers. This letter is similar in purpose to the multilateral escape clause which is included in the GATT and it is similar in its terms to a letter which forms part of our separate trade agreement with Japan.
When I first announced this new agreement, I made clear that it will not affect our strategic export controls. A provision is included which recognizes that either government may apply prohibitions or restrictions of any kind for the protection of it's essential security interests. This provision would take precedence, if necessary, over any other provision of the agreement.
One of the clauses in the agreement refers to the treatment of merchant ships. This clause was studied very carefully before we agreed to include it. The practical effect is to give a continuing assurance to the Russians, for a period of three years, that their ships will continue to enjoy in our seaports such as Vancouver as favourable treatment as the ships of other countries. In other words, the provision simply confirms the kind of treatment which has been available all along to ships of U.S.S.R. registry.
I should also say something about the provisions which refer to the legal status of persons, access to courts and arbitration. These do not establish any new procedures for settling disputes that might arise in the conduct of trade between Canada and the U.S.S.R. They merely indicate the facilities that are available if any such disputes should arise. These provisions will, no doubt, be recognized as useful to traders and trading organizations in both countries. There is nothing in this agreement that might force Canadians to go before Russian courts, rather than to Canadian courts, nor force them to choose arbitration for the settlement of disputes. I mention this because there might otherwise be some misunderstanding about these particular provisions on the part of people who may not have had an opportunity to examine the legal problems which are involved.
From the Canadian point of view, by far the most important part of this agreement is the letter by which the government of the U.S.S.R. guarantees to purchase and take
Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. delivery from Canada, during the three years of the agreement, a total between 1,200,000 and 1,500,000 metric tons, i.e. between 44-1 million bushels and 55-1 million bushels of wheat, in annual lots of between 400,000 and 500,000 tons, i.e., between 14-7 million bushels and 18-4 million bushels. The exact amounts to be purchased in the second and third years, within these annual amounts, will be determined by the government of the U.S.S.R., taking into account the volume of Soviet goods sold to Canada. The total over the three years, however, will amount to not less than 1,200,000 tons and the amount in any individual year will not be less than
400.000	tons. The Russian purchases of wheat are to be made at the prices and on the terms at which the Canadian wheat board is making sales to its major customers at such times as the Soviet purchases take place. The U.S.S.R. has already purchased mcfre than
400.000	tons for delivery during the present year.
The agreement is written to terminate at the end of three years. At that time the two governments could agree to extend it. The conditions governing an extension would have to be worked out in the light of our experience in the three-year period.
I shall not attempt to predict to what extent there may be a long term demand for Canadian wheat in the U.S.S.R. This agreement provides a demonstration that the government is prepared to move vigorously, on commercial terms, into any market that develops. If there should prove to be a continuing market in the U.S.S.R. that we can satisfy, then we shall be all the more pleased. To the extent that it is possible to do so, we are establishing ourselves in a good position at present. It is reasonable to expect that there will be at least some continuing basis for Russian purchases of wheat from this continent, even if that country should not be short of grain. From the point of view of transport, it is cheaper to ship wheat across the Pacific to far eastern ports of the U.S.S.R. than to transport it overland from the major wheat growing areas in western Russia.
As for other Canadian commodities, it may well be possible to develop trade in nonstrategic goods that the U.S.S.R. needs and that are competitive. The very fact that a trade agreement has been concluded indicates perhaps a willingness on the part of the U.S.S.R. to trade more with this country. To a very large extent, Canada and the U.S.S.R. export similar things. The potentialities of trade, while valuable we hope to both countries, would thus seem to be fairly limited. I do not wish to create the impression, therefore, that there will be a large market in

Russia for very many Canadian products. At the same time, it is realistic for exporters to be alert to such opportunities as may develop and to take advantage of them.
My colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) will no doubt wish to take part in this debate. I would like to refer particularly to the part he played in making this agreement possible. During his trip to the U.S.S.R. late in 1955, the Secretary of State for External Affairs initiated the discussions on trade which led later to the negotiations which took place in Ottawa.
I am informed that the U.S.S.R. was represented by able experienced officials who conducted themselves throughout the negotiations in a straightforward, businesslike manner.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S.S.R.-APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 29, 1956
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker*, it is a coincidence-and I am sure not more than a coincidence-that the government is presenting to the house this afternoon for ratification this trade treaty with Russia on the day that Premier Bulganin and Mr. Khrushchev are arriving in Great Britain for a widely heralded visit which has attracted the attention of the western world.
It is natural that at the outset, when the house is invited to ratify such an agreement, we should ask what steps have been taken by the other party to the treaty to ratify it. We are told that under the Russian practice the signing of the agreement by their authorized officers itself constitutes ratification on the part of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. In submitting the agreement to both houses of the Canadian parliament for ratification and approval the government is following Canadian constitutional practice. I think we will prefer it to the Russian practice.
The elements of this agreement have been clearly stated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) on two occasions, namely on February 29 and today. The agreement is accompanied by an exchange of four letters, two from each of the parties to the other. In approaching the resolution now under debate I take it that we are entitled to look at all five documents, for certainly the letters have extremely high importance for us in our approach to the question of ratification and approval of the treaty.
The minister has indicated that the treaty gives to each of the parties unconditional most-favoured-nation treatment. It is an agreement that is to run for a course of three years. There is no automatic extension provided. Extension is permitted only if the parties agree on such extension within a period of three months prior to the expiration of the three-year period on February 28, 1959.
rMr. Howe (Port Arthur).]

The agreement and the letters contain safeguards and there is, of course, the important collateral agreement on the part of the U.S.S.R. to purchase Canadian wheat.
I should like to embrace this opportunity of paying tribute to the Canadian officials in whose hands the negotiation of the treaty was placed. We do not have many opportunities in the house to express our tribute to competent public servants to whose hands great responsibilities are committed. In the Department of Trade and Commerce there are some outstanding officials in whom I am sure all parties of this house have confidence when important responsibilities such as the detailed negotiation of such an agreement as the present one are placed in their hands. There were difficulties in the way of arriving at any kind of agreement. There were the difficulties of misunderstanding. There were the difficulties of hostilities that had been created over a period of time and there were language difficulties. There were the difficulties involved in breaking new economic ground. In arriving at any agreement under those circumstances, and in the face of those difficulties, I am sure the house recognizes the important and thoroughly praiseworthy work of competent officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
I suppose the minds of some of us are naturally carried back today to May 12, 1954. In many respects the business on which the house is engaged this afternoon is reminiscent of the business that engaged the house on the date to which I have referred. It was the day on which parliament was called upon to ratify the trade agreement with Japan. There we were dealing with a nation which had been a late antagonist in the war, and at the hands of whose armed forces and authorities many Canadians had suffered unspeakable cruelties. Yet, sir, we had to recognize that there were not only important economic interests at stake in our trade relations with Japan but also far-reaching political issues and involvements in the kind of world in which we have to live in this postwar era. We saw on that occasion a trade relationship with Japan under which Canada was enjoying substantial advantages, and we saw also the strategic position that Japan holds in the Pacific, particularly in view of the way in which the communist rule had marched to the coast of the mainland. So we in this house by, I think, unanimous decision resolved that it would be a good thing for Canada, indeed a good thing for the world, if Canada and Japan entered into that trade agreement.
In approaching the question of a trade agreement with Russia there are some factors that are different from those that entered

into our thinking in connection with the Japanese trade treaty. There are others that are common to both. We have not had the extensive trade and economic interests in common with Russia hitherto that we had with Japan at that time. Our political relationships with Russia are very different from those which the western world has sought to establish with Japan in the postwar period. On the other hand, we are not unmindful, sir, that while Russia was our ally in world war II, and Japan was our mortal enemy, nevertheless in this postwar period we have been living in the era of the cold war. We are not unmindful of the crimes of the Kremlin which have been perpetrated upon suffering mankind in the past decade and more. Nevertheless, sir, recognizing the existence of these crimes, virtually all of which are yet unatoned, we think that there is merit in the present measure.
Let us examine the extent of our trade and economic interests with Russia so that we may see in their true proportions the economic interests of which this treaty takes account. Our trade with Russia has been almost insignificant in amount for some time past. I give you, sir, the figures on Canada's export to Russia for the past four years. In
1952	it amounted to $421; in 1953, $478; in 1954 there was an increase to $4,854,311; in 1955, a reduction to $2,680,153. The major items in our exports to Russia in 1954 were pulp sulphite, canned meats, barley and cattle hides in that order. In 1955 our leading exports to Russia consisted of pulp sulphite and nonedible vegetable oils. We exported no barley to Russia in 1955.
On the import side I offer these figures for the same period. In 1952 we imported from Russia goods to the value of $2,234,413; in
1953	the figure dropped to $824,007; in 1954, it dropped further to $687,081; and in 1955 it dropped further to $628,156. Our imports from Russia in those years consisted almost entirely of fur skins. It will be seen, then, that our trade with Russia has been insignificant in amount in recent years.
It would be well for us not to expect perhaps too much from the agreement now under discussion. The minister has said this afternoon, and of course correctly, that it will depend on the alertness of the salesmen of Canadian goods to their opportunities in the Russian market. It is true it will depend upon that factor, but our sales to Russia will depend on a great many other factors as well, not the least of which will be government policy in the U.S.S.R. I noted with no little interest that when I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in the house on February 29 as to what might be 67509-193
Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. expected in the way of trade his answer was extraordinarily cautious. My question, sir, is found at page 1662 of Hansard. It was put to the minister at the conclusion of his statement, and reads as follows:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister what is the best estimate of the dollar value of the import and export trade that is expected under the terms of this pact?
The minister's reply was:
Mr. Speaker, I said once before that I had lent my crystal ball. I am afraid I cannot give the hon. member an answer.
Now, when we find the Minister of Trade and Commerce taking refuge in a reply as cautious as that one, we cannot fail to be impressed, because that is rather unlike him. Therefore, I say, sir, that it would be well for us, I think, not to attach too much hope to a wide extension of trade with Russia as a result of this agreement, or to read into it particular political significance.
May I say, sir, that it is the intention of Her Majesty's loyal opposition to support the present motion for ratification of the agreement, and I should like to put that support upon several broad grounds. In the first place, sir, this is an agreement whose purpose is to provide for an extension of trade. Articles 1 and 2 of the agreement give full effect to the principle of unconditional most-favoured nation treatment. We have subscribed, as I believe all political parties in this house have subscribed, to the principle of multilateral trade. We in this part of the house have had occasion to complain, as we do still complain, that the government's trading policies have resulted in a dangerous concentration of our external trade. Therefore, we are glad to welcome any extension of trade on a true multilateral basis.
In the second place, sir, we regard, as I have no doubt all political parties in this house regard, trade as an important asset in establishing conditions which will make war more and more distasteful to nations. The hope of establishing commercial relationships is associated in the minds, I am sure, of all hon. members with the desire to see more links created among nations of the world that will make peace advantageous to them and to create at the same time more reasons for making war more and more disadvantageous to them. And so, while we have not changed our views in regard to certain aspects of our possible trade with Russia- and I am referring now particularly to trade in strategic materials-nevertheless, we do subscribe, as I am sure all hon. members do, to the view that the closer commercial relationships become in the world the greater is going to be the incentive to peace.

Trade Agreement with TJ.S.S.R.
In the third place, sir, the prospect of selling Canadian wheat to the U.S.S.R. is naturally an important factor weighing to the advantage of the present agreement. We have, under the agreement that is collateral to the main pact, an undertaking on the part of the U.S.S.R. to make purchases of Canadian wheat of undesignated grades in those next three years, a guaranteed minimum of
400,000	metric tons per annum, or, expressed in terms with which we are more familiar, 14-7 million bushels per annum. And, then, there is the over-all guarantee of the purchase of 1,500,000 tons of wheat in the 3-year period, which is, in the figures with which we are better acquainted, 55-1 million bushels. The price will be the price prevailing at the date of individual sales and, under the agreement, is to be the price at which Canada, through our wheat board, is selling to other large foreign purchasers.
In his reply to questions on February 29 the minister stated that the wheat that the U.S.S.R. is to take represents a fair distribution over our milling grades of wheat. Sir, we have in Canada such a huge surplus of wheat that any opportunity at all to sell a significant portion of it is bound to commend the co-operative support of hon. members.
In the fourth place, sir, among those reasons why we support the present motion for ratification and approval is the group of safeguards that are contained in the agreement and the accompanying letters. The minister has referred to those today as escape clauses. For my part, I prefer to call them safeguards, and there are five in particular that I think are deserving of comment.
In the first place, there is clear provision in the second paragraph of article 3 of the treaty for the retention by Canada of full power to take whatever steps may be necessary in relation to strategic materials. That paragraph reads:
The provisions of the present agreement shall not limit the right of either contracting party to apply prohibitions or restrictions of any kind directed to the protection of its essential security interests.
Sir, that, in the view taken by Her Majesty's loyal opposition, is a safeguard of vital importance; for, without such a safeguard, I do not suppose it would be possible for parties in this house to support the agreement.
Now, the definition of strategic materials is not static. It has undergone revision from time to time since the western nations were first called upon in the Korea and post-war Korea period to take steps to place embargoes upon the sale of strategic materials to countries behind the iron and bamboo curtains.

There may be further changes in store, changes that I say should only be brought about in the closest association and consultation with the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States of America; but that there must, in the conditions still prevailing in the world today, be restrictions and embargoes upon the shipment to countries behind the iron and bamboo curtains of certain strategic materials is, in my submission, incontestable. Therefore, sir, I attach the highest degree of importance to that first safeguard.
The second of those five safeguards is the right reserved to the Canadian government to apply special duty values. This right is reserved, not in the formal terms of the agreement, but in the first of the accompanying letters by which the Canadian government reserves the right to fix, under the Canadian Customs Act, values of goods for ordinary and special duty under certain defined terms where Russian goods are imported, or are likely to be imported into Canada:
... in such quantities and under such conditions as to cause or threaten serious injury to domestic producers of like or directly competitive products.
In such cases the right is clearly reserved to the Canadian government to fix values for ordinary and special duty purposes.
There is always the concern and fear in matters of this kind when a country under a free economic system enters into trading agreements with a country operating on a state trading basis, particularly a communist country, that there is every likelihood of the dumping of the goods of the communist country in the other country. We have had some experience in Canada with tactics of this kind. We will not forget the situation of two years ago when we had such an experience with goods imported from Czechoslovakia. Hon. members will not, I am sure, forget the experience of the western world with Russian dumping in the thirties. This particular safeguard is therefore also of the highest importance and the house will be entitled to demand of the government in relation to this safeguard the strictest vigilance to assure that Canada will not be permitted to become a dumping ground for undervalued Russian goods.
The third of these five safeguards, sir, is the preservation of the commonwealth trading preferences. Under article 7 there is clear provision that the agreement, providing as it does for unconditional most-favoured-nation treatment, is not to have any application to the "exclusive advantages accorded by Canada to members of the British commonwealth of nations, including their dependent territories, and to the Republic of Ireland".

The fourth of these safeguards relates to Canada's exchange position and balance of payments, for under the first paragraph of article 3 of the agreement we have the clearest provision that while no prohibitions or restrictions are to be applied by either contracting party on goods imported from the other, nevertheless a clear exception is made in this article for "import or exchange restrictions applicable to all countries in like circumstances for the purpose of safeguarding the external financial position and balance of payments". In the kind of world we are living in, safeguards of that kind have become imperative.
The fifth of these safeguards, sir, is contained in article 4. I do not attach any great value to this particular safeguard but I mention it for the purpose of making a comment upon it. Under this article the merchant vessels of each contracting party and the cargoes of such vessels shall, upon arrival at and departure from the seaports of the other contracting party and during the time spent in such seaports, enjoy the treatment accorded to the most favoured nation.
Now it is quite obvious that the wheat sold to the U.S.S.R. by Canada under the terms of the letters accompanying the agreement will move via the Pacific, no doubt from Vancouver to Vladivostok on the Russian side of the Pacific. We have already seen press comment on the fact that one Russian ship loaded wheat at Vancouver for shipment to Russia since the agreement was entered into. That is all very well, sir, but it would be of more interest to Canadians if there were some prospect of Canadian bottoms being used for the shipment of this Canadian wheat from Canadian ports to Russia. This is one place where, had the government not permitted the Canadian merchant navy to evaporate in post-war years, there might have been a real opportunity for Canadian bottoms to share in the advantages that might be hoped for from these shipments of Canadian wheat to Russia.
We in Her Majesty's loyal opposition attach great value to these safeguards and particularly to the first four which I mentioned. Their value will, of course, depend upon the use that is made of them and that in turn is going to depend upon Russian government policy; but it will depend as well on the vigilance of the Canadian government.
There is no indication as to what commodities the U.S.S.R. will endeavour in particular to sell to the Canadian market. It would have been of interest to us to have had some indication; indeed, it might have offered some hope of additional safeguard where it seems to me some safeguard is required. I think 67509-1935
