Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. it to be deplored, sir, that there is no guarantee in this agreement that Canada shall not be asked to import goods manufactured by forced labour behind the iron curtain. By this agreement it is entirely left to Canadian purchasers to assure themselves if they choose to do so, that the goods they are purchasing from Russia are not goods manufactured by forced labour.
In the second place, sir, I should like to remind hon. members of the inherent dangers of state trading. It is inevitable, when trading between two nations is done either on one part or on both parts on the basis of state trading, that political dangers will be inherent in these trade relationships and any rupture of them that may follow. Look at the problem of enforcing contracts; look at the problem that the Canadian exporter faces in selling to state purchasing organizations in the U.S.S.R. Suppose contracts are cancelled; suppose there is a default in payment or in performance of contractual obligations on the part of the Russian state trading organization. Should this happen, is there going to be any effective redress? Well, sir, I do not think anyone can be too confident that under those conditions there will be any effective redress whatever.
It is not many months ago that a good many manufacturers in the United Kingdom thought they had reason to cheer when wider trading relationships were established between the United Kingdom and Soviet purchasing organizations, but a good many of them faced a rather disturbing and disillusioning experience not long after when a great many of the contracts were cancelled by the Russian purchasing organizations and these British exporters learned to their dismay that they were without any effective redress. Let us not forget that there are also serious political dangers inherent in state trading and in particular in state trading with communist countries.
The third matter to which I draw attention follows from the last one I have mentioned and relates to article 5, under which Canadian citizens and other natural persons domiciled and carrying on business in Canada and juridical persons constituted in accordance with the laws in force in Canada are to be entitled in the U.S.S.R., in respect of persons and their property, to treatment on a basis no less favourable than that accorded to the natural and juridical persons of any other state.
Let us be realistic. I doubt very much whether the government is going to say that in the light of experience, in the light of well recognized facts, there is very much comfort or assurance for Canadian exporters

Trade Agreement with TJ.S.S.R. in provisions of that kind, in relation to well-known Russian judicial procedures.
The fourth matter to which I draw attention, in trying to bring about a sound and fair understanding of this agreement and what it contains, as well as its limitations, is the danger that wherever Russian trade organizations go there is always the danger of espionage. I do not need to remind hon. members of the experience that Great Britain had with Russian trade organizations in the 1920's, when they thought they were engaging in beneficial mutual trade. We in Canada have had enough experience of our own, in regard to the use that Russia has made in times past of diplomatic relationships, to put us on our guard against the inevitable danger that is inherent in Russian plans of any kind of using channels of this kind for espionage purposes.
Having attempted that appraisal of the features of this agreement, let me say in conclusion that all of us, I am sure, must try to see this agreement in its true perspective in relation to the whole world-wide context of today. Russian political and economic tactics are inscrutable. Nevertheless, this agreement may, at least on superficial view, fall into its place in a pattern with which we are becoming familiar, a pattern that is not, in many of its elements, unwelcome in the world today, a pattern that we have associated with the so-called postGeneva period of the past ten months.
Whatever may be the true purpose of Soviet policy in relation to these facts, we have witnessed a number of extraordinary reversals of Russian tactics in this period. One thinks of the exchange of visits of diplomats and the press; of the Austrian treaty, with the withdrawal from Austrian soil of Russian forces of occupation; of the release by Russia of the bases which it held in Finland; of the current denunciations of the memory of Joseph Stalin; and, within the past 48 hours, the announced disbandment of the Cominform.
Whatever in the Geneva spirit and the post-Geneva period has resulted in consequences such as some of these-and I mention in particular the Austrian treaty, which of course is welcomed as a contribution to the relaxation of international tension-at the same time hon. members will not have forgotten that the Geneva conference was followed, within a very short time, by the visit to India by Mr. Bulganin and Mr. Khrushchev and the series of lies and falsehoods that characterized their speeches to the Indian people in relation to the western powers.


Hon. members will not have forgotten either that the point of greatest tension in the world today in the Near and Middle East stems from the sale by Russia and Czechoslovakia of arms to Egypt and other countries and Russia's adamant refusal to curtail those shipments of arms in the interests of the relaxation of tension and the threats of war in that vital and disturbed area.
It will not be forgotten that it still remains the policy of the Kremlin to stir up trouble against the west wherever opportunity offers. We will not have forgotten that the concentration camps are still flourishing in Russia, that the satellite countries are still under Russian occupation and that personal liberty is suppressed in all those countries.
Whatever tactical changes may have contributed in certain quarters to the easing of the tensions, we have no reason to think that there has been any change in the deep-seated and fundamental aims of the Kremlin policy. Those aims remain as they were defined long ago: world revolution and world domination by the Kremlin.
I am sure all of us in this house will wish to be on our guard against being misled into doing something that fits in with some change in Russian tactics, the purpose of which simply is to weaken the resistance and the will on the part of western nations to stand firm against the dangers that Russia has created to the peace and security of the free nations of the world. We well know that the purpose of Russian blandishments in the past ten months has been to the fullest extent possible to weaken NATO and the will of the western nations as expressed in NATO. There have been some evidences, some perhaps disturbing evidences, of the success of the Russians-disturbing from our point of view -but we may be hopeful, and we may at the same time, I think, discharge our duty to be realistic.
Canada, like all the western nations faced with a decision such as we are called upon in this Canadian House of Commons to make today, cannot in the face of our world duty take a deliberately unfriendly course. It is a duty of the western nations, in the kind of world we live in today, while being realistic, to avoid taking deliberately unfriendly courses. When an opportunity offers to make any contribution toward easing tensions in the world today without any loss of essential interests on the part of our country, then I conceive it to be our duty to take that course.
We have not forgotten the young Canadians who lie in Korean graves today, whose sacrifice is attributable to aggression that was,

if not ordered, at least abetted by the Kremlin and the government with which this treaty has been negotiated. Hope is a virtue but it is our duty, while being hopeful, to be realistic. Therefore if I may attempt to define in a word the view that we take in supporting this trade agreement with Russia I would say this: we believe that Canada should try, in the world of today, to be friendly and at the same time to be vigilant, to be realistic, to keep our guard up and to keep our powder dry.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S.S.R.-APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 29, 1956
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has said, I have no doubt that this treaty will receive the unanimous approval of the house. I hope that in the course of the debate the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) will accept the invitation extended to him by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to participate in the debate. May I also suggest that I think the house would appreciate hearing a word or two in the same connection from the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) in the course of the discussion of trade with Russia because he too had opportunities to see the internal conditions of that country.
I also want to join in the well deserved tribute paid by the hon. member for Eglinton to the officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce. You know, from time to time in the house we hear about the bureaucrats and what they have or have not done, and it is refreshing that we are able at times to express our appreciation of the work which has been done by the permanent officials of the departments who serve not only their departments but the country so well. The Department of Trade and Commerce has such officials within it to whom we can pay that tribute.
I was very happy indeed to accept the invitation extended by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the luncheon he gave when he entertained the Russian negotiators and also to accept a subsequent invitation from them to dinner in the Chateau Laurier. I think that those of us of all parties who met them on those two occasions will realize that they were a very able group of men. Not only are they a very able group of men but individually they are charming and cultured men, and if they were wholly representative of the Soviet union what a better place this world would be than it is today.
I am one of those who have made some study of the history of the past and sometimes when I have listened to speeches that have been made regarding relations between the western world and the Soviet union and have
18, 1956	3047
Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. read our newspapers and our literature I have been very forcibly reminded of some of the literature, history and speeches of the 30 years following the French revolution when France was as great a bogey to the countries of western Europe as the Soviet union is today. When I say "bogey" I do not mean something that is not real, because I think that in those days the leaders of the French revolution did threaten the very basis of the society of western Europe.
But as time passed the tensions eased, and little by little the western Europeans and the French were able to accommodate themselves to their different republican and monarchial views. So, perchance, we are now witnessing the evolution in the world-I hope this is so but I will not say I am sure of it-of the accommodation of the two differing points of views that are so prevalent in the world today and that at last, perhaps over a very long period of time without war, we may manage to live together and to find ways and means of co-operating more and more. I say that because this, I think, is one of the methods by which better understandings, the easing of tensions and mutual co-operation for the common good can be brought about.
We in this party have long urged that we should try to trade with countries that we say are behind the iron curtain. I should like to see not only the recognition of the fact that there is a new government in China but also trading channels opened so that we might be able to exert some influence within that country and offset to some extent the reliance of that country on the Soviet union. Because I believe these things I am very happy indeed to congratulate those who negotiated the treaty, to express to the government our support of the agreement and to say that I am quite sure that both economically and politically it will be beneficial to us and to the world at large.
There are, of course, as has already been pointed out both by the minister and by the hon. member for Eglinton, difficulties in negotiating treaties of this description with countries with trading organizations that are so different from our own, and I think it is good that in this particular instance those difficulties were overcome. I have no doubt that in coming to this agreement the negotiators for the Soviet union intend and the government of that country intends, as we intend, to carry out the agreement and to give it full effect for our mutual advantage.
As a member representing a constituency that is vitally interested in the marketing of grain, I am very glad to note that, while it is not written into the agreement, agreements were reached for a substantial sale
3048	HOUSE OF
Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. of the commodity upon which the prosperity of my own constituents and, let me also say, to a very large extent the prosperity of this country, really depends. It was once said in the house, I believe, that no group of people in a measurable period of time had produced so much new wealth for this country as the people who homesteaded, who took up land on the western plains and put that land under the plow. That was true in those days and it is true today although not to the same extent because our forest industries, mining industries and manufacturing industries have forged ahead in recent years.
However, it is still true that a very large number of people and a very large section of our economy depend upon the ability of this country to market wheat at a price that will return to the producer not only the cost of production but a sufficient amount to enable him to maintain a good standard of living and to buy the goods that he needs in order to keep our manufacturing industries going fully ahead. Therefore, from the point of view of the economy of Canada, and particularly from the point of view of a western member of parliament, the agreement to take quantities of wheat, a minimum quantity and a maximum quantity under the conditions outlined, is indeed something which makes this treaty very attractive to us.
I could not help thinking this afternoon how this agreement is now being received in this house. I remember that a year ago there was considerable criticism in this house and in the country in some quarters because of the government's sale of some 9 million bushels, I think it was, of wheat to Poland and of the financial arrangements that were made at that time. I have no doubt that the Poles benefited from the acquisition of that wheat and that our export organization will be paid in full for the wheat as under the agreement the payments are required. I think that was a beneficial deal and I think, of course, this one is even more beneficial. There is, of course, one feature of the agreement that we must keep in mind. While we -talk of the maximum amount of 55-1 million Ibushels of wheat, we must remember that that maximum amount is dependent upon Canada's taking goods from the Soviet union. In the words of the understanding, the amount to be taken during the second and third years of the agreement shall be finally determined with due account being taken of the volume of sales of Soviet goods in Canada and Canadian purchases thereof.
As has already been said, we have no indication as to what those goods may be. I do not know what the Russians can send


to us. As we have been told, they have been sending furs to Canada. But we are a fur-producing country ourselves. I do not know what other commodities we can obtain from Russia to the benefit of the Canadian economy and to our mutual advantage-our special advantage being, of course, that we are able to sell the maximum amount of wheat. Perhaps, as the debate goes on, we might have some suggestions as to what the government had in mind as to the commodities that might be imported into Canada. Of course it was fully understood that the commodities which came into Canada would not be dumped here. Mr. Borisov, the leader of the delegation, acknowledged receipt of Canada's reservation of the right to establish its own value for duty on any Russian product which might enter Canada in such increased quantities as to cause serious difficulty to Canadian industry. In the same way we protected the valuation of the commodities that we might import.
To my mind this agreement is of primary importance not only to the wheat producers, not only to Canada but indeed in a large measure to the rest of the world as indicating a willingness to trade and perhaps as a contribution to the easing of the tensions in the world today. This agreement gives the right, of course, to traders from Canada to go to Russia to sell their commodities and for Russian agents to negotiate in Canada with our people who may be inclined to buy commodities from Russia, and provides for their entry into our respective countries and their protection under the laws that govern our own nationals and their nationals. Whatever we may think of those laws within Russia, at least we are on the same basis as far as the words of the agreement go. But I should like to see something beyond this. For example, I should like to have seen the parliament of Canada, through Mr. Speaker, accept an invitation for parliamentarians to visit that country and for Canada to receive a similar delegation from that country. I should like to see cultural exchanges between these two countries. I should like to hear Russian musicians and I should like the Russians to hear Canadian musicians. I should like to see Russian ballet; and I should like to see our Winnipeg ballet have an opportunity, if the exchange were made, of performing in the Soviet union. I think that nothing but good could come from the opening of these channels that have been closed to us over the years.
One is not obliged to accept the ideology of an individual in order to have friendship. Within this country we have sharp differences in our approach to philosophy, sometimes in our approach to religion and in our

approach to social thinking. Yet within our country we are able to respect one another's views and to live together in unity. I think the day will come when that statement will be true with respect to the entire world. As I said earlier in my remarks, I hope that what we are witnessing is an evolution across the world in that direction. We are wrong if we think in blacks and whites. We must recognize the fact that between the extreme of the one and the extreme of the other there is a line that is rather fuzzy and grey. But the very fact that that line is there is a hopeful sign and gives some assurance that we may at last be able to understand each other just a little bit better.
I am not going to go into the details of the agreement. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) went into the safeguards in it and expressed his views with regard to them. In discussing a treaty of this description I do not believe it is wise to promote anything in the nature of ill-feeling and suspicion. I think we should stick to the terms of the treaty itself and the benefits that we expect to derive from it. I hope that it will work out to the advantage of Canada. Of course I also hope that the Soviet union will receive benefits from it. However, I hope primarily that it will be beneficial to us in this country. In so far as we have been able to secure the sale of what is quite a large quantity of wheat, I am sure it will be beneficial. The wheat will pass through Vancouver, so we are told. Hence it will assist the port of Vancouver. It will go from Vancouver to Vladivostok because the Russians say quite openly-and I think quite properly-that it is cheaper to transport Canadian wheat from Vancouver to Vladivostok than it is to ship wheat from the Ukraine and the wheat fields of Russia by rail to Vladivostok in order to feed the people who have become established in eastern Siberia.
I do not intend to pursue this matter further, Mr. Speaker, except to say that we support the signing of this agreement and express our appreciation to the competent officials-and indeed to the government which employs them-for having negotiated a treaty which I believe will be of benefit to Canada and will assist in easing tensions across the world.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S.S.R.-APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 29, 1956
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we look upon this trade agreement as a straight business deal and one that may be of advantage to both parties concerned. Under the agreement each party accords the other unconditionally most-favoured-nation treatment but article 7 provides that this shall not apply, or perhaps I should say is not to
Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. interfere with the exclusive advantages accorded by Canada to British commonwealth nations. In addition certain reservations were made by Canada to prevent serious injury to her domestic producers. Whilst that provision was not actually in the agreement it was in a letter written by Canada to the U.S.S.R. and I understood the minister to say that the letter is actually part of the agreement.
It looks to us to be a very fair agreement. I believe, or perhaps I should say I hope, that it may help to liberalize the thinking and the views of the Russians who come to this country. No doubt some people will say to me that I am indulging in wishful thinking, but on the other hand if we give up that hope in matters of this kind we indeed face a bleak future.
Now, at the time of the signing of the agreement the U.S.S.R. agreed to buy from us between 1,200,000 and 1,500,000 metric tons of wheat over a period of three years at a rate of between 400,000 and 500,000 tons a year. I thought the clause governing the difference between the 400,000 and 500,000 tons that the U.S.S.R. may buy in the second and third year to be a very sensible one. This provision reads:
The quantity of wheat between 400,000 and 500,000 tons purchased by the Soviet union during each of the second and third years of the validity of the agreement shall be finally determined with due account being taken of the volume of sales of Soviet goods in Canada and the Canadian purchases thereof.
Personally I think that is a very sound principle. I should like to see a principle of that kind embodied in practically all the trade agreements that we have with other countries. I think it would be a very good thing if we could have that principle embodied in the trading relations between this country and the United States because if that were the case we would not today be suffering from an adverse balance of trade in the neighbourhood of a billion dollars. This is a sound principle because it does recognize that trade is a two-way street and that we should at least be prepared to buy a certain amount of goods from them if they buy from us. It is true that the amount of wheat provided for under the agreement signed after the trade agreement was established is not very large. It is between 40 million and 50 million bushels in round figures. After all, though, a number of deals for 40 million or 50 million bushels would add up to a very considerable sum and would certainly help to move the surplus wheat. I am satisfied that this agreement will be supported wholeheartedly in western Canada.
3050	HOUSE OF
Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R.
There is no doubt that there is some fear regarding article 5 of the agreement. This article provides that Soviet citizens, when engaged in business activities in Canada, will be accorded the same favourable treatment as accorded the citizens of other states and the U.S.S.R. reciprocates in regard to Canadians in the U.S.S.R. The point upon which I should like to hear the Minister of External Affairs speak, when he does speak, is as to whether or not the treatment given by Russia to citizens of other states is as favourable as the treatment that we will give to the Russians when they come to this country. I understood the minister to say that this will be no different from any other agreement that has been made with other countries. However, I believe that past experience has been that Canadians over in Russia have not had anything like the degree of freedom that perhaps we have allowed Russians in this country. I understand that situation is improving and I hope it may improve still further in the future.
We welcome this new market for wheat from which we will receive Canadian dollars or United States dollars. It will no doubt help us with our problem in regard to the United States. I am glad also to have the assurance that no strategic materials will be shipped. It is rather difficult these days, I think, to define exactly what strategic materials really are because so many foods actually can be used in the manufacture of munitions. On the other hand, I do realize that there are certain goods which can be very definitely classed as strategic materials and those materials will be barred from shipment.
I am also interested in the question that has been asked the minister concerning what commodities are most likely to be exported by the U.S.S.R. to Canada. I hope he will give us a little bit more information on that. I am hoping that we may get some interesting commodities because we have heard so many boasts from Russia that they were the first nation to produce this or that. I am hoping we will get some of these "firsts" shipped over here, some new commodities we have never seen before. No doubt if that proves to be the case there should be quite a wide market in this country for commodities of that type.
I think also it would be a good thing if we could buy from the U.S.S.R. some of the things we are now buying from the United States. In that way we might help to reduce our imbalance of trade with that country. I believe the minister, himself, will agree that our trade with that country is now top heavy. If we can do anything to encourage


the purchase of commodities from nations on the other side of the Atlantic instead of buying from the United States, it would be a good thing for this country and might encourage the United States to buy a little more liberally in this country.
I hope also that we will have some words from the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) regarding his experience while he was in the Soviet union. I have read some interesting accounts of some of his experiences, and I am sure all of us in this house would enjoy hearing them at first hand. In closing, I would say we intend to support the agreement because we do believe it will be of advantage, not merely to Russia, but very definitely to the farmers of this country.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S.S.R.-APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 29, 1956
speechtext:
In
the first place I should like to congratulate the minister and his officials upon their brilliant negotiation of this splendid trade agreement. I should like also to commend the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) for his constructive approach to this agreement and for the very many salient facts he brought out about trade with the Soviet union. The crux of the matter is, of course, that Russia wanted to buy our wheat and that we had the wheat to sell. In other words, this wheat market may be of incalculable value to Canada. I think that is the basis of the agreement and the point we should keep in mind.
It is a very favourable treaty, I would say, to both sides; but naturally we are interested in it primarily from the Canadian point of view. I think there is a great deal to be said for this agreement. The hon. member for Eglinton pointed out that in 1954 Canadian exports to the U.S.S.R. amounted to $4,854,000, and in 1955 to $2,680,000, and that the products exported were mainly pulp sulphite, canned meats, barley and cattle hides. It will be noted, Mr. Speaker, that there is no mention of wheat because we did not export wheat at that time. If one considers the minimum per annum to be shipped under the agreement, one will see that 14 [DOT] 7 million bushels of wheat per year will be exported; and if one takes the price of $1.25 per bushel as a minimum, it will be seen that we will be receiving about $18,375,000.
When one considers that our imports from the U.S.S.R. in 1954 and 1955 were respectively $687,000 and $628,000, one will see that this agreement will result in a very substantial and favourable balance of trade from the Canadian point of view. That is extremely good, Mr. Speaker, and as the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) has just pointed out, it will take care of our imbalance with other countries to some extent.
I should like to point out it is conceivable that the market established for wheat in the

U.S.S.R. may provide other markets. I have in mind particularly butter, of which Canada is a considerable producer, and second, farm implements. Hon. members will know of the trip to the U.S.S.R. recently made by Mr. James Duncan, president of Massey-Harris. It is to be hoped that other Canadian businessmen will establish and expand their contacts with the Soviet union. I understand that last year only $10,000 worth of farm implements were sold to the U.S.S.R., but conceivably this could be greatly expanded, particularly when one considers the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that it is cheaper to export, say, wheat from the west coast of Canada to Vladivostok than to take it across the Soviet union. Conceivably it would also be cheaper for the Russians to buy farm machinery from Canada than it would be to take it across from European Russia.
Finally I might compliment the minister also on what the hon. member for Eglinton called the safeguards, or the escape clauses, in the agreement. Of course we all realize the importance of making sure that strategic materials are not shipped to the U.S.S.R. It is also equally important that, as a result of this agreement, unfair competition should not result to Canadian producers and manufacturers. I think the minister has taken care of that in the agreement in every possible way.
I concur in the views of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that it is desirable to expand our cultural relations, and that any economic and social intercourse between the Russian people and the Canadian people is all to the good. We all appreciate our way of life, and any kind of communication with the Soviet union is certainly to be desired in promoting world fellowship and to ease world tensions.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the minister and his officials who carried out the negotiations so brilliantly in connection with this treaty.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
subtopic: CANADA-U.S.S.R.-APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 29, 1956
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are one or two brief comments I should like to make on this particular resolution. There is no legislation which has come before the house in recent years which will be more welcomed in western Canada. I think the minister and his officials should feel very gratified today. This is an excellent business deal for Canadians.
I welcome this agreement for two particular reasons. In the first place, it is going to sell a substantial portion of our western wheat surplus to the Russians, as I understand it about 45 million bushels over the next three years. I think it is a good agreement also, because any kind of trade agreement between the east and west tends to
Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. strengthen mutual relations and understanding among the peoples of the world. I hope this agreement is only a prelude to other agreements which our government will make with iron curtain countries. At this moment I think particularly of China.
I would like today to give a little advice to the Russians. If they really want to increase their trade under this agreement they might emulate in certain respects the people of the United States. I think they might consider making certain investments in Canada. Generally speaking, trade follows investments. We have heard a great deal in the last week or so about foreign investments in this country. Some people profess to see something sinister in these investments. As I see it, nothing could be further from the truth. If the Russians have a little extra capital that they would like to put into our country, perhaps it could be used to advantage by Canadians.
In the field of investment and trade it seems to me that we Canadians must recognize certain basic economic facts. Our post-war boom has been based largely on foreign investment, mainly American. If it were not for that investment I do not suppose we would have such projects as Arvida, Kitimat, Ungava, International Nickel and Steep Rock, much of our oil development and the like.
I am sure most thinking Canadians are delighted that there is such a large influx of outside capital coming into this country.
I cannot get very worried about the fact that foreign countries have established subsidiaries in Canada, whether they are Dutch, Belgian, Russian, or American. They employ Canadians; they use Canadian materials; they pay Canadian taxes, and they are helping to develop our country. I think outside companies, particularly American, have invested in Canada not because they want to dominate our country but simply because, as investors, they see a chance to make a lucrative profit in Canada. God help the employment picture in the Dominion of Canada if those countries, especially the United States, should suddenly stop the kind of investing they have been doing in the past 10 years.
There is another field where I would suggest the Russians might emulate the people of the United States, and that is with respect to the activities of Ambassador R. Douglas Stuart. In my opinion Mr. Stuart was one of the best ambassadors ever to be sent to Canada. I think he has done an excellent job. There has been criticism of a speech he made recently in Vancouver. It seems to me that all he was doing was talking elementary common sense. He gave us a few hard economic facts in a friendly way, and I do not think we should resent them. Mr. Stuart has
3052	HOUSE OF
Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. carried out his duties well and when he leaves Canada, in my opinion, our country will lose a real friend. Therefore I say to my Russian friends, perhaps they would do well to emulate some of the activities of Mr. Stuart.
This resolution could open a new era in Canadian trade. I believe the treaty will be advantageous to both countries.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S.S.R.-APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 29, 1956
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will start with a comment made by many an hon. member in this house, that I had no intention of entering this debate; but both the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Acadia suggested that because I had been in Russia last summer I should make some comment.
My visit to Russia last summer was primarily a visit that had to do with whaling and fisheries. I have reported to my colleagues in the cabinet on the things I learned there, and have made very long reports to the scientists of our fisheries research board, to the senior officers of my department, to the fisheries association of British Columbia and to the fishermen's union of British Columbia on the fisheries aspects of my visit. When my estimates were before the house I told hon. members that I was more than willing to appear before the standing committee on marine and fisheries to report and be questioned on those aspects.
However, I was in Russia for two and a half months, much longer than I expected to be there, and did have the opportunity of crossing the country from the Baltic sea to the Pacific ocean, and then north to the Bering sea. In that time I had the opportunity to appraise in my amateur way what trade possibilities there were. I must agree with the earlier comments of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that at the moment there do not seem to be very many fields in which we can engage in a mutually profitable trade.
There are pretty obvious reasons for that. We are both northern countries. Well, that is not quite right. We think of Russia as a northern country, but it came to me as somewhat of a surprise when I was there and studied the maps to see how far south Russia does go, down to the boundaries of Persia and Afghanistan. They produce almost all their own cotton, for example; they produce all their own tea, but in general they have the same northern resources as we do.
One of the things that impressed me most of all was the tremendous amount of untouched natural resources, especially in Siberia. Therefore we cannot expect very much of mutual trade in natural resources. As far as the other great block of trade in 

which this country engages is concerned, consumer goods, I think it is generally known that Russia is very short of consumer goods. The living standards of their people are considerably below the standards of people in the western world, and since they have not enough consumer goods for their own people I think it unlikely that we can develop our trade in consumer goods from them.
The field wherein we have an opportunity for trade as far as exports from our country are concerned is in foodstuffs. Hon. members have already commented with favour on the arrangements made by this treaty for the sale of a considerable quantity of Canadian wheat to Russia. I think perhaps we may also have an opportunity of selling fish products. Russia today is the second largest fishing nation in the world, but they are net importers of fish. Canada is the sixth fishing nation in the world but actually we are the second largest exporter of fish in the world. I hope that perhaps when the Russian minister of fisheries is in Canada this summer we can explore the possibilities of exporting fish to Russia. Iceland today has a very satisfactory export fisheries trade with Russia.
I believe, however, in this matter of exporting foodstuffs to Russia there is a point which my hon. friends should not overlook, and that is how intensely productive free farmers and free fishermen are. This country with a population of 16 million people produces an abundance of food not only for its own people but can afford to ship foodstuffs to Russia, a country of 225 million people which has such enormous resources but which, under collective development, certainly has not been able to achieve the productive record of our free society.
I am of the opinion that the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton and the speakers who followed him concerning this particular treaty are right. This treaty does represent the opening of a new door, and certainly if we have a free exchange especially of our businessmen in Russia seeking trade opportunities, undoubtedly more trade will develop. This will be greatly to our own advantage, of course, because of the special conditions in the wheat agreement providing for minimum sales, and providing that sales will increase according to the level of purchases from Russia which are made by the Canadian trade.
When I was in Vladivostok on the way out, the mayor of Vladivostok came to see me and asked me to send a wire to the mayor of Vancouver. It was an extremely interesting wire, in which he expressed the hope that trade relations would be resumed in order

that both these great Pacific ports could [DOT]enjoy the sort of trade they had some years ago. I very gladly sent that wire. In that particular the mayor of Vladivostok was not very different from the mayor of Vancouver or the mayor of any other Canadian town who wants to see the development of his home city. Actually I believe the wheat is going to leave from Vancouver, which is a very good thing for that port. Possibly it is going to be received in the new Russian port of Nahodka, some 70 miles north of Vladivostok. Vladivostok is now primarily maintained as a naval port.
I would like to agree, too, with the other speakers that this is more than just a trade treaty; it is a very positive step forward in trying to build up better understanding between ourselves and the Russian people.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S.S.R.-APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 29, 1956
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very pleasant occasion when hon. members of all parties are so unanimous in supporting the resolution before us. I shall try not to interject any sour notes in my remarks. I feel that the Minister of Fisheries who has just resumed his seat and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have performed a most valuable public service not only for Canada but for the entire western world in having visited the U.S.S.R. last year. I am convinced that if it had not been for their visits this resolution would not be before us this afternoon.
I say this is a good thing for the western world, because I think our two ministers have made some contribution toward the establishing of better understanding. I believe a great deal is to be gained by exchanges of ideas. Everyone will, I think, agree that these two ministers are probably in a better position to point up to the Canadian people our important values which we must always maintain. In spite of some unfriendly Canadian performances, I think that the Russian farmers who came to Canada last year went back home feeling that the Canadian people on the whole were somewhat different, and perhaps a little better than the people they expected to find here.
I have a great deal of sympathy for the Minister of Trade and Commerce as he proceeds to develop this sort of trade. My sympathy stems as a result of some of the things which have been said and done by hon. members in this chamber. I was thinking of an occasion a week ago yesterday when for no apparent reason the Leader of the Opposition took it upon himself to refer to the visit to Great Britain today of Bulganin and Khrushchev and the visit to that country a short time ago of Serov. While I am not permitted to quote the exact words used to
Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. refer to people we cannot change or do anything about, I am convinced that referring to them as butchers, thugs and murderers, and referring to those who employ Serov as being in the same category, must make it more difficult for those who are negotiating further trade with the people in the country concerned.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration a week ago today, when my leader raised the question of Paul Robeson being barred from Canada, said he thought hon. members should be well aware it is not the policy of the government to admit known communists to this country either as immigrants or visitors. Now, Mr. Speaker, I think the Canadian people are quite competent to meet and hear and see whom they will, without the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration employing that sort of language.
This brings me to the sort of problems we are going to have to face very soon. This agreement provides for the firm sale of some 44-1 million bushels of wheat during the next three years. It also provides for the sale of 55-2 million bushels which will be sold on the condition that certain goods are admitted to Canada from Russia. There is a difference between the two figures of approximately 11-1 million bushels.
At this point I want to say that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is an extremely lucky person. When we were discussing some of these problems earlier in the year I am sure the minister had no information to the effect that Europe was to face a disastrous winter which would create such a large demand for Canadian wheat. We rejoice with the minister in that our surpluses are now going to be depleted to a large extent, but I think the minister must not lose sight of the fact that in spite of the unfortunate and disastrous winter in Europe every major wheat-producing country in the world has embarked on a subsidized program which will result in large surpluses of cereals in years to come.
Consequently a country such as Canada, which has depended to a large extent upon the export of cereals, must now pay attention to deals like this under which we can sell an additional 11-1 million bushels of wheat during the next three years providing we buy some goods from Russia. It is not going to be easy to bring in from Russia sufficient commodities to balance that sort of transaction without causing some inconvenience and some disruption to certain Canadian industries. Nevertheless, I think it is in the public interest that we face the fact that these new problems are on our doorstep, and I think they can be solved.
To illustrate the sort of problem that arises, may I give the following illustration. Last
3054	HOUSE OF
Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. year when the Polish deal was announced I was naturally interested, because our Saskatchewan economy is very closely tied up to wheat and my constituency is particularly interested in the port of Churchill. I was anxious that some wheat, if possible, might move through this port, so I contacted the Polish legation here to find out whether their attention had been drawn to the very decided advantages there would be in having wheat go out through Churchill.
It was too late to get any of it moving last year, but this year I have had some discussions with the people at the Polish legation who have been negotiating these contracts, and their proposition is very reasonable. They point out that they are going to be in the market for wheat for the next ten years at least, and that they probably could buy $10 million worth of wheat from Canada per year if we would increase our purchases from Poland from very little to $5 million.
Their experts who were working on it realize that they cannot expect to sell us wheat, butter or bacon. They have made a very careful study of our imports and the countries from which we import. They pointed out that since we have an unfavourable balance with the United States, we might consider buying from Poland some of the goods which they are prepared to sell, instead of from the United States.
Last year cement was one of those commodities. Last year we had to buy quite a large amount of United States cement and pay a very high premium for it. Polish cement did not get into Canada. This year negotiations were under way again for Polish cement. I happened to meet, at one of those social affairs where members meet people from all over the world, one of the Polish people who had been working on this problem. I asked him how our wheat sales had been going and how the Canadian wheat was measuring up to standards. Apparently our grade 5 wheat blends very satisfactorily with their wheat. They are well satisfied.
I asked how our trade was. That was not so good. It was explained to me that the expert who has been negotiating is a lawyer who does not know much about cement. The competition is very keen, and they were anxious to bring in two cement experts, but they were having some trouble in getting visas to allow them into Canada. I suppose the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is very particular about who comes in and who stays out.
I said, "If I can be of help, do not hesitate to let me know". They were very pleased with the courtesy that has been extended to them by the Minister of Trade and Commerce


and his staff. They explained that it was better to have these things done through the regular channels, and I agreed. I said, "If you find you are going to lose sales or you cannot get by, give me a call".
The day before I went home for Easter I received a call. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was away at Washington. I discussed the matter with one of his officials and pointed out that at some point they had to say yes or no to this sort of request, and I did not think it should take a month to decide whether or not two cement experts should be permitted to enter Canada. However, when I came back after the Easter recess I found that a decision still had not been reached. I think six weeks is too long to take to reach a decision as to whether people should be admitted into Canada.
Whilst one minister of the crown says that hon. members are well aware it is not the policy of the government to admit known communists to the country, I think we would be surprised if any experts from Russia were not communists. I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not take that point of view when he was asked if he would permit a trade delegation to come to Canada.
I submit that if we hope to be able to sell the additional 11-1 million bushels of wheat involved in this particular transaction, somehow or other we have to be able to clear the applications that come from people who are involved in these transactions. If we do not want them to come that is our business, if we do not want trade, but I think every member who has spoken in this debate has agreed that this particular transaction is certainly in the national interest of Canada. I am sure it would not be completed if it were not in the national interest of Russia, and I am sure that in the years to come we are going to be obliged to have dealings with people who do not go to the same church, who do not have the same coloured skin as our Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, or who do not happen to hold our particular political views.
When you go into your store at home, the manager of that store does not ask these questions. I submit that in this day and age, when we are trying to ease world tensions and trying to promote trade, some of the speeches that have been made in the house and outside the house might well have been left unsaid.
Before I conclude I wish to say again that I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Fisheries have made this transaction possible, and they deserve high marks for it. I wish the Secretary of State for External Affairs would act

on the suggestion I have made on a number of occasions, that provision be made for the visit of an all-party delegation from Canada. I am sure it would not do any harm and might do some good. There are other industries in Canada, in addition to the wheat industry, that might be interested in an exchange of ideas. The fact that Mr. J. S. Duncan, president of the Massey-Harris Company, a world-wide organization, took time out of a very busy life to go to Russia and spend some time there does suggest that those of us who are charged with looking at the over-all economy of Canada might follow the example set by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Fisheries.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADA-U.S.S.R.-APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 29, 1956
speechtext:
Before the motion carries I might say a few words in connection with it, and deal with one or two points that have been raised. This discussion, which has shown, I think, that there is unanimity in all quarters of the house that the motion should "be carried and that the treaty should be ratified, as one which will be to the advantage of our country; may even carry with it some political, as well as economic, advantages.
The question of the background of the negotiation of this treaty has been raised. The negotiation of the treaty goes back to last autumn, when an invitation was extended to me to visit the Soviet union. I was asked at that time what I would like to see and what subjects I would like to discuss with representatives of the government in Moscow. After consultation with my colleagues, it was suggested to the authorities in Moscow that one of the subjects would be the development of trade between our two countries. For that purpose an official of the Department of Trade and Commerce accompanied me to Moscow. Possibly, Mr. Speaker, I can add at this time my tribute to that which has been paid by others to the excellent work done by that official, the associate deputy minister of trade and commerce, and other officials of that department and other departments of government, including external affairs, who were concerned with this matter.
These preliminary discussions in Moscow made it clear that there was a reasonable possibility of negotiating a mutually advantageous treaty between the two countries. We made it clear in Moscow, before the negotiations were referred back to Ottawa, that there could be no inclusion of materials on our strategic list in any trade negotiations and, on the other hand, that we would expect a commitment from the Soviet government for the purchase of wheat. It was also made clear in Moscow that the negotiations should
18, 1956
Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. be resumed in Ottawa and brought to a conclusion, if possible, here. As the house knows, that was done.
The Soviet government sent a team of trade experts to Ottawa where there was quite a serious and indeed at times difficult negotiation of details of an agreement, with eventual success. It was found by those on our side that those who were representing the Soviet union were competent, straightforward and frank negotiators and, as has been mentioned already this afternoon, personally very agreeable people to deal with. I think we can take satisfaction that the negotiations have resulted in the treaty which is now before the house.
There were difficulties, of course, as would be natural and, indeed, inevitable when negotiations are taking place between representatives of countries which are so different economically, politically and in every other way as those of the Soviet union and Canada. Some of these difficulties were honest ones arising out of misunderstandings of constitutional procedures. For instance, we are today asking the House of Commons to approve ratification of this treaty. In Soviet practice no such approval is, of course, required and, indeed, legally and constitutionally under our own system no such approval is required because ratification is an executive act. It was hard to make the Soviet representatives understand that while legally the executive could ratify and the agreement could go into effect at once, it was our constitutional practice-and a very good practice it is-that no international treaty or agreement of any significance at all, whether political or economic, should be ratified by the executive without the approval of the legislature.
This particular agreement, Mr. Speaker, is substantially the same as those which we have in the field of trade and commerce with most other countries. For instance, for some years we have had most favoured nation treaties with Poland and Czechoslovakia. It is true that these arrangements were made before the communist party took over the governments of those two countries, but the treaties remained after the governments became communist. No special difficulties have been found in the application of the treaties since that time and they have, I think, been of value to our country. There are a good many trade agreements of this type between the Soviet union and western countries, including the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Austria and the Scandinavian countries. It is true there is no such agreement between the United States of America and the U.S.S.R. but hon. members will know, of course, that the administration in Washington is now

Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. seeking congressional authority to dispose of surplus agricultural products to the Soviet union.
I think it will be agreed that this agreement is advantageous to our country in the field of trade and commerce. I think it will also be agreed that no wider Canadian interests, political or economic, are likely to be jeopardized in any way by it. It certainly does not make us unduly dependent, for instance, on the Soviet union as a market for our wheat. Desirable as it is to find markets wherever we can it would, I think, create some uneasiness if this particular market were too large in relation to our total sales, but there is certainly no danger of that happening under this agreement. As hon. members know, the commitment in any one year will amount to between 15 million and 18 million bushels of wheat, which is comparable to our exports to Belgium or to the Federal Republic of Germany, and compares with a figure for last year of 31 million bushels to Japan.
During the course of the discussion the question has been asked, what commodities are we likely to receive from Russia as a result of the trade which we hope will develop between the two countries? That, of course, is a very difficult, indeed an impossible question to answer, especially in the case of trade between two countries in one of which trade is conducted under our system of individual enterprise and free initiative and in the other by a state trading organization. But, as has already been pointed out, production is developing, production is growing in the Soviet union, and it may well be that during the course of the agreement it will be possible for the initiative of Canadian traders to express itself in the development of trade, including imports from Russia, which will be of benefit to this country. I myself have no idea in what direction that trade will move but it is, I think, certainly safe to say that we are beginning a new era of trade development with a country which is already showing increasing strength both in the field of industry and in the field of agriculture.
While it is perfectly true, as my colleague the Minister of Fisheries has pointed out, that under our system of free enterprise and initiative our per capita production capacity is much greater than that of the inhabitants of the Soviet union or, indeed, of other communist states because of the nature of our social and economic organization, nevertheless while that may be true per capita the figures for production in the Soviet union in recent years and the planned figures for the next five years are very impressive indeed. In this connection may I quote some remarks made by the president of the Massey-Harris


Company who visited the Soviet union last year, as members know, and who has made some very interesting reports on his visit since his return. In a speech in Ottawa not many weeks ago he said:
Agriculture is one of the weakest spots of the Russian economy. The process of regimenting the peasant, dispersed as he is over large areas, with his natural yearning for the ownership of a piece of land, and his greater independence and individuality than the city worker, has proven to be a difficult nut to crack.
But I do not wish to weary you with details. I will go no further than to state that, to our eyes, the Russian system of agriculture is undermechanized, bedevilled by bureaucracy, cumbersome and wasteful of manpower.
But he went on to say this:
The vitality and drive of the Russian dictatorship and of its people is, however, clearly illustrated in this field also-
That is the field of agriculture.
-by the fact that during the years 1954 and 1955, they brought under the plow 70 million acres of virgin land, an area so vast that it exceeds by 10 million acres the size of the United Kingdom.
Then, as to what had been done in the field of industrial production he had this to say:
Thus it is that having largely recovered from the damages of war, Russia's economic strength has taken a great step forward during the past five years, and you may have seen in the press only a few days ago that her new five-year plan includes an all-out drive to increase her industrial production by 1960 to two-thirds of the U.S. figure for 1955. In this plan, Russia now declares that she has it within her means to become the world's mightiest industrial nation. Having observed the manner in which Russia in the past has met and frequently exceeded her five-year objectives, I am not prepared to shrug off these recent assertions as being mere boastfulness.
That is what Mr. Duncan says. He continues:
Do not let us forget, when one considers the amazing increase of Russian industrialization in recent years, that it is based in no small measure upon the good old premise of hard work, to which we also used to be dedicated. Much can be accomplished by a nation where all men and all women work 48 hours a week.
So, Mr. Speaker, when we are approving a trade arrangement with the Soviet union we are approving an arrangement with a country which is making great strides forward in industry and in agriculture. There are political as well as economic implications in that fact.
It may be asked-indeed it has been asked, though not in this debate-whether the Soviet union will carry out the obligation which it has undertaken to Canada with respect to wheat purchases. I think we may have confidence that it will do so. Selfinterest, if no other reason, would dictate that it should do so. Apart from its need for wheat, a failure to do so would damage its international reputation in trade matters,

and it would appear to be a little bit more sensitive about that reputation now than it was some few years back. Certainly we would regard any failure to fulfil its wheat obligations as a violation of the trade agreement itself. The exchange of letters re purchase of wheat is as binding-and it is understood to be so-as are the articles of the agreement itself.
It should also be emphasized-and this has been pointed out also this afternoon, more particularly by the hon. member for Eglinton-that in this agreement there is nothing which would prejudice in any way our security interests because of the safeguards that have been written into the agreement. It may well be that because of this agreement the Soviet union may wish to set up in this country certain trade facilities for the carrying out of the agreement, more particularly the obligation to purchase wheat. For that purpose it may wish to open a trade office in this country.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the government has already received from the Soviet government a request to that effect, namely for the opening of a small trade office more particularly for the purpose of purchasing wheat. That request is now under consideration and a decision with regard to it will be taken very shortly. No request has been made for the opening of any office with diplomatic privileges or immunities, and the government would not be disposed to agree to the establishment in this country of any diplomatic office outside of the embassy in Ottawa.
Trade is one field in which it is possible for us to bring about at this time a more normal relationship with the Soviet union without prejudice to our own security or our own ideals, and without diminishing in any way our close association with our friends in other parts of the world. In this treaty we are not, of course, giving the Soviet union anything that we have not at least in equal measure given to all friendly countries long ago. It would have been unreasonable, in my opinion -and I think this opinion is shared in all quarters of the house-for the Canadian government to have failed to take advantage of this opportunity to enter into a sensible and useful agreement. I think we would have been open to justifiable criticism from responsible and moderate people, both here in Canada and abroad, if we had turned our backs on the possibility of a reasonable working relationship with the Soviet union in this field.
We all long for the day when there may be sufficient mutual trust that reasonable arrangements of this kind, even with communist countries, not only in trade but in many
Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. other fields, will become the rule rather than the exception. If this trade agreement and the experience of both countries with its operation over the next three years help toward that end by reducing suspicion, we shall have good cause to be satisfied with it on political as well as economic grounds.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S.S.R.-APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 29, 1956
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a few words on this agreement. First of all may I say that, like all other hon. members of this house who have spoken thus far, I am in favour of the agreement. I do not desire to sound any discordant note, but the agreement raises a problem which must trouble other hon. members of the house. I refer to the problem that is raised of diplomatic and trade relations with a country the principles of whose government we abhor.
I represent a riding in the city of Toronto that probably contains more ethnic groups than does any other riding in Canada. It has been my pleasure to be closely associated with the leaders of a number of those groups, and I am familiar with the views they hold with regard to Russia. In my riding there are representatives of ethnic groups from the Baltic countries of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. I need only remind hon. members of the house that it was in 1940 that the Russians invaded those countries when Germany was attacking Poland. They were driven out of some of those countries by the Germans, but the Russians re-established themselves in 1944.
I mention these facts only to indicate the depth of the feeling that is entertained by the people who come from these countries. The same hostility is felt by people who have come from Poland and Czechoslovakia, and by people who have come from the Ukraine and Byelorussia, both of which at the present time are parts of the Soviet union.
We ask ourselves how these conditions came about. We know that the conditions were created because of aggression by the U.S.S.R. We know that one principle adopted by the U.S.S.R. at the present time, as a natural consequence of communism and atheism, is hostility toward religion. We have seen evidence of persecution of churchmen in all these countries. We know the U.S.S.R. now has its paid agents and fellow

Trade Agreement with U.S.S.R. travellers in every democratic country whose sole object is to subvert the democracies in which they are living. We know also beyond doubt that the ultimate object of communism is domination of the world.
Everyone is in favour of improving our relations with Russia, but it is my respectful submission to the house that lasting improvement in these relations can only be based upon the principles of justice. It is not possible to have a system of justice prevailing until the peoples in those countries have been given the opportunity of getting the kind of government they want, and not the government that is forced upon them by the U.S.S.R. There cannot be justice until the slave camps have been abolished in the U.S.S.R., and we will never feel at ease until it ceases to be the policy of the U.S.S.R. that they will endeavour to subvert the democratic countries.
May I just say this, that while I welcome the agreement I hope it will not have the effect of lulling us into acceptance of the injustices we know exist in the U.S.S.R., and that we may use the better relations that may be established as a means of working toward the removal of these evils.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CANADA-U.S.S.R.-APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED AT OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 29, 1956
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say
just a few words, and in doing so I join in the chorus of approval that is being expressed for the agreement, ratification of which is now before the house.
I do not wish to repeat any of the arguments or points that have been made, but there do seem to me to be one or two things that might yet be said. I have been interested in the statements made from the government side to the effect that, though the negotiations in the end were successful, they were not without their difficulties along the way. I can well imagine that there were a number of difficulties, not only because of the language problem but because of the different approach to trading that obtains in our two countries. I can imagine that, just as in any sort of bargaining each side wants to get the best possible deal, undoubtedly that would be the case in these negotiations. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, the fact we are witnessing today is that these negotiations, serious and difficult though they have been along the way, were at last successful.
One does not want to read too much into any result such as that, but I think we should take hope from the fact that it is possible, in the very difficult field of trading, for the representatives of our nation and of the Soviet union to sit down and work out an agreement which is mutually satisfactory. Let us hope that means that by persistent


effort, by practising the virtue of patience, by determination, we may yet achieve better and more satisfactory relations between our two countries in other fields for the good of mankind and for the peace of the world. I hope that what we are discussing today is only a step in the direction of improving relations between our two countries.
I have been interested also, Mr. Speaker, in the comments made by the Minister of Fisheries and the Secretary of State for External Affairs concerning the standard of living that now obtains in the Soviet union. The Minister of Fisheries referred to the scant volume of consumer goods he found in that country. Both he and the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to the low productivity per capita that obtains in Russia as compared with the productivity per capita of our Canadian economy. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was quick to point out that though the per capita productivity may be lower in the U.S.S.R. their absolute productivity in terms of volume is of course very great.
As one who, like the two ministers and Mr. J. S. Duncan and others, had the privilege, although 10 years ago, of spending a few days in the Soviet union, I am interested in the reports that have been made by those who have visited that country more recently. I felt then, as these gentlemen do now, the sense of vitality and drive, the vigour of the people, despite what the Minister of Fisheries said about the standard of living of the people being low by comparison with our standards in this country. When I was there that was certainly true in such things as food, clothing and shelter, though as I reported to this house after my return from that visit in 1946 one had to admit that the Russians were in a different world when it came to the theatre and the cultural field. The interest of these people in those things is much greater than their interest in food, clothing and shelter, and that interest was being expressed in many more of them getting advantages of that kind than is the case here.
What I wanted to say particularly, Mr. Speaker, was that I think we would be deluding ourselves if we were to assume that the low volume of consumer goods which obtains in that country will always be the case. It certainly was the case when I was there and the Minister of Fisheries says it is the case now. One of the many interesting visits I had while there was to a Soviet factory in Moscow. My father was a railway machinist, and I know something of what machines look like in a factory. I knew the kind of machinery I was inspecting in that factory. It consisted mainly of lathes and planers. I asked

through an interpreter what this factory was producing and I was told it was producing mainly lathes and planers. Then I asked where this heavy machinery was being sent, and to what use the lathes and planers produced in that factory were to be put. The answer was that they were being transported to other factories which were to make more lathes and more planers.
I wondered, of course, when some consumer goods would come out of the process.
I was told that along the way there were certain things produced, but only in limited quantities. In fact in this very factory which was producing lathes and planers they were producing a few baby carriages. There seemed to be quite a contrast between the heavy character of the lathes and planers and baby carriages. The point was that their main interest at that time, and I take it from the Minister of Fisheries it probably still is so, was not in consumer goods. Their main interest was in more and more machinery to produce still more machinery.
Surely what we must realize is that one of these days that process of mechanization will reach the point where they will start to produce consumer goods. When they do that volume, as we can imagine, will be of tremendous proportions. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when that day comes, when their system permits or arranges for people to start to have more consumer goods, it is going to be to the advantage of Canada or any western country, to have already established trading relations with these people.
My guess would be that when that day comes they will in the main produce their own consumer goods. But since we recognize that trade is a two-way street, that trade is a means whereby we can both profit, we producing the goods that we can produce most economically, and another country doing the same, it seems to me it is quite possible that the day may come when to the advantage of the Russian people and to the advantage of any other nation that is trading with them, there could and will be trade in consumer goods.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that we would be following the part of wisdom, both for our own standard of living and for theirs, and thereby for the good of mankind and the peace of the world, if we would develop, on the basis of the agreement that we have now established, further trading relations, and if we would keep active and alive the kind of negotiations that have been carried on leading up to this agreement which the house is now prepared to ratify.
I join in the commendation that has been paid to Mr. Sharp and others who did the
Committee on Atomic Energy main part of the work in connection with these negotiations. I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce will keep other people alert on the job so that as conditions change in that country, as change they will, we shall be in on the ground floor for trading relations in these other fields.
Toward that end, Mr. Speaker, as well as for other reasons mentioned, for the good of the peace of the world, for more understanding amongst our peoples around the world, I support the plea that has been made again today by the hon. member for Mackenzie to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that there should be more visits back and forth between that country and this, including visits by members of parliament.
I think exchanges of visits by other people from other walks of life would also be important and valuable both for us and for them.
I hope that what we are doing today will suggest to the government that more thought should be given to this as well as to what I have already suggested, namely a continuing interest in the possibility of developing trade relations with this country in other fields.
I am sure we all agree that in this way, the way of trade, the way of seeing more of each other, the way of mutual understanding, the way of raising the standards of living in our countries the world around, lies the possibility, if we will make use of it, of establishing a more secure peace for mankind. On that basis I join with all the others who have spoken in supporting the motion which is now before the house.
Motion agreed to.
