subtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
subsubtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN NON-MILITARY RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order to conclude my remarks before six o'clock I shall be very brief and condense the remarks I had intended to make at this time.
As on other occasions, I feel that the resolution before the house proposes to deal with
3080	HOUSE OF
Committee on Atomic Energy a very serious problem in a rather unsatisfactory way. A committee has been suggested which has been stripped of the powers necessary to do the type of job which we feel should be done at this time. I know Your Honour will take serious objections if I reflect on the vote on the amendment to this particular motion, but I think the fact the committee is not able to send for persons, papers or records seriously handicaps it in the type of work which we think it should carry out.
There are one or two other disappointing aspects to the debate on this resolution. The first I feel is the lack of enthusiasm on the part of the government. I feel that they were constrained to proceed with the setting up of this committee by pressure from the official opposition group, and that having set up this committee they think they have discharged their responsibilities in this particular field.
I am also disappointed in the approach to this problem as expressed by Conservative speakers. I have read very carefully the remarks which hon. members to my right have made, and I have concluded that their main argument is that the government ought to be giving greater assistance to private business in the field of research. I have come to the conclusion that that is the burden of their arguments; that private business wants further assistance from the government, and that as far as they are concerned they see this particular move as a means of reaching that objective.
When the hon. member for Broadview spoke in this debate he referred to the United Nations report published last January showing the percentage increase in manufacturing production, and he placed on record some very interesting figures. The figures indicate that in the 6-year period from 1948 to 1954 the percentage increase in manufacturing production in Japan was 230 per cent; in West Germany, 205 per cent; in France, 38 per cent; in India, 36 per cent; in the United Kingdom, 33 per cent; in the United States, 22 per cent; and in Canada, 17 per cent. These figures are very interesting, but the inference I draw from them is that private business has not been doing the job. It is an indictment against the free enterprise system. What he is saying, in effect, is that since Canadian business has failed to keep pace with industrial research it is up to the government to get into the field and give it a further handout.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that is the main burden of the argument presented by members of the official opposition. If we look at the role of the government in research I think we shall find that already business


in Canada is getting very substantial assistance in the way of tax concessions. They are in a position to carry on research work in order to keep pace with business in other parts of the world. We know that in recent years corporation profits' have increased to such an extent that there is no reason why Canadian business cannot spend more money on research.
Every time the old age pensioners, or persons on war veterans allowances or pensions, come to the government and ask for additional assistance, they are lectured by the spokesmen of private enterprise. They are told that it is demoralizing to accept government help, yet the amazing thing is that when it comes to government assistance, assistance from the public purse, the industrialists of this country are out there with both arms thrown wide and fingers open waiting for assistance.
As far as the national research council is concerned, I noted in their report for 1954 that during that year 7,500 technical inquiries had been made on behalf of private business in Canada at the taxpayers' expense. The point I am trying to make at this time is that rather than looking upon the research program merely as a means of providing greater assistance, or additional assistance, to private business, we ought to be looking upon the research program and the effect it is going to have on the country as a whole.
I think many spokesmen for business have expressed similar points of view. I note that in a recent issue of the Financial Post Dr. Stratford, who is I believe the president of the research council of Ontario, pointed out that there is very little industrial research being done by private business in Canada. He points out that in his opinion not more than a half dozen Canadian firms are doing a proper job of research; yet many of these firms that are doing little or nothing in the field of industrial research are spending fortunes on advertising and so-called public relations. Their profits have increased greatly in the post-war years.
It seems to me that if corporations are increasing their profits they have an obligation to spend more of their income on research. The shocking situation revealed by the hon. member for Broadview when he spoke a few days ago in quoting the United Nations report that Canada lags far behind the other nations of the world in respect of industrial research indicates the failure on the part of Canadian business to meet its obligations.
Hurrying along, Mr. Speaker, I should also like to refer to a statement made by Mr. B. M. Brophy, who I believe is a former deputy

minister of trade and commerce. In an article which appeared in the Financial Post on June 11, 1955, Mr. Brophy said:
Canadian dependence on foreign research and development is too well known to need emphasis. Indeed it can be argued that much of our industrial development has been the result of the know-how provided for us by the parent companies of our foreign based concerns.
A little later in the same article he says:
We should have no quarrel with this arrangement for obtaining know-how, in our present circumstances, but is it adequate in the light of our ambitions? Is not a more appropriate approach warranted to this problem of obtaining such a vital ingredient of industrial progress? Should we not inject some plan and purpose into our own managerial thinking? After all, Canadian requirements in the field of research and development are not identical with those of other countries.
We have here a spokesman for the Ontario research council, a man who was high up in the government a few years ago, telling Canadian business the same thing. It is time the business interests of this country stepped up their own research programs, yet we find that the main burden of the argument proposed by some hon. members in this house is that the government's role in the field of research should be to give additional assistance directly to private interests.
As Canadians I think we are extremely proud of the role of our national research council. I believe the work they have been doing is quite indicative of the greater service which they could render to Canada if their facilities were greatly expanded. It is not necessary for me to burden the house with statements made by various individuals from time to time pointing out the fact that we are falling behind in turning out scientists and technicians from our universities. It is quite obvious that while the national research council must be the focal point of any research program in this country, we have to have a broadly based program, and that means giving greatly increased direct assistance to our universities. I realize that the national research council has made grants and that these amounted to $2,500,000 in 1954, but this is a paltry amount in terms of present needs. Any research program must be based upon the Canadian educational system. We have to provide for a greater flow of high school graduates into our universities in order that we might do a more effective job. It seems to me that this is the main role of the
Committee on Atomic Energy government in a research program. I think Canadian business with its increased profits and with the tremendous expenditures which are made on advertising could well afford to spend a greater part of its income in the field of applied research.
As far as our research program in general is concerned, I suggest that it has to be broadly based. This brings up something which we have been arguing for a long time. It involves federal assistance to education in Canada. It seems to me that we are not going to have our young men and women entering universities unless we have high school graduates, and high school graduates depend upon our whole educational set-up.
As I have already said, we in Canada feel justly proud of the work done by the national research council although I think its employees are grossly underpaid. I suggest that as a result of their low salaries they are indirectly subsidizing Canadian industry. A great number of inquiries have been made by private businesses in Canada, and they have been accommodated to a large extent by the national research council. Since the employees of the council receive very low salaries, salaries far below those which they deserve, they are in effect providing a substantial subsidy to private industry. If we are thinking in terms of a research program I think we will have to provide more adequate remuneration for those Canadians who are taking part in that program.
I have some other remarks I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, but unless another hon. member wishes to speak I shall conclude my remarks now to facilitate the taking of the vote.
Motion agreed to.
